The Filtration Induced by a Locally Nilpotent Derivation

Bachar ALHAJJAR Address: Bachar ALHAJJAR, Institut de Mathématiques de Bourgogne, Université de Bourgogne, 9 Avenue Alain Savary, BP 47870, 21078 Dijon, France. Email address: bachar.alhajjar@gmail.com
Abstract.

We investigate the filtration corresponding to the degree function induced by a non-zero locally nilpotent derivations ∂\partial and its associated graded algebra. As an application we provide an efficient method to recover the Makar-Limanov invariants, isomorphism classes and automorphism groups of classically known algebras. We also present a new class of examples which can be fully described with this method.

Introduction

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero, and let BB be a commutative kk-domain. A kk-derivation ∂∈Derk​(B)\partial\in\mathrm{Der}_{k}(B) is said to be locally nilpotent if for every a∈Ba\in B, there is an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that ∂n(a)=0\partial^{n}(a)=0. An important invariant of kk-domains admitting non-trivial locally nilpotent derivations is the so called Makar-Limanov invariant which was defined by Makar-Limanov as the intersection ML⁡(B)⊂B\mathrm{ML}(B)\subset B of kernels of all locally nilpotent derivations of BB ([3]). This invariant was initially introduced as a tool to distinguish certain kk-domains from polynomial rings but it has many other applications for the study of kk-algebras and their automorphism groups ([4]). One of the main difficulties in applications is to compute this invariant without a prior knowledge of all locally nilpotent derivations of a given kk-domain.

In [5] S. Kaliman and L. Makar-Limanov developed general techniques to determine the ML\mathrm{ML}-invariant for a class of finitely generated kk-domains BB. The idea is to reduce the problem to the study of homogeneous locally nilpotent derivations on graded algebras Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{Gr}(B) associated to BB. For this, one considers appropriate filtrations ℱ={ℱi}i∈ℝ\mathcal{F}=\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{R}} on BB generated by so called real-valued weight degree functions in such a way that every non-zero locally nilpotent derivation on BB induces a non-zero homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation on the associated graded algebra Grℱ​(B)\mathrm{Gr_{\mathcal{F}}}(B).

In particular, every kk-domain BB admitting a non-zero locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial comes equipped with a natural filtration by the kk-sub-vector-spaces ℱi=ker(∂i+1)\mathcal{F}_{i}=ker(\partial^{i+1}), i≥0i\geq 0, that we call the ∂\partial-filtration.

In this article we show that this filtration is convenient for the computation of the ML\mathrm{ML}-invariant, and we give general methods to describe the sub-spaces ker(∂i+1)ker(\partial^{i+1}) and their associated graded algebra.

Knowing this filtration gives a very precise understanding of the structure of semi-rigid kk-domains, that is,kk-domains for which every locally nilpotent derivation gives rise to the same filtration. For such rings the study of the ∂\partial-filtration is a very efficient tool to determine isomorphism types and automorphism groups. We illustrate how the computation of ML\mathrm{ML}-invariant of classically known semi-rigid kk-domains can be simplified using these types of filtration. We also present a new class of semi-rigid kk-domains which can be studied with this method.

1. Preliminaries

In this section we briefly recall basic facts on filtered algebra and their relation with derivation in a form appropriate to our needs.

In the sequel, unless otherwise specified BB will denote a commutative domain over a field kk of characteristic zero. The set ℤ⩾0\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} of non-negative integers will be denoted by ℕ\mathbb{N}.

1.1. Filtration and associated graded algebra

Definition 1.1.

An ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration of BB is a collection {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} of kk-sub-vector-spaces of BB with the following properties:

1- ℱi⊂ℱi+1\mathcal{F}_{i}\subset\mathcal{F}_{i+1} for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} .

2- B=∪i∈ℕℱiB=\cup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i} .

3- ℱi.ℱj⊂ℱi+j\mathcal{F}_{i}.\mathcal{F}_{j}\subset\mathcal{F}_{i+j} for all i,j∈ℕi,j\in\mathbb{N} .

The filtration is called proper if the following additional property holds:

4- If a∈ℱi∖ℱi−1a\in\mathcal{F}_{i}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{i-1} and b∈ℱj∖ℱj−1b\in\mathcal{F}_{j}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{j-1}, then a​b∈ℱi+j∖ℱi+j−1ab\in\mathcal{F}_{i+j}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{i+j-1}.

There is a one-to-one correspondence between proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtrations and so called ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree functions:

Definition 1.2.

An ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function on BB is a map deg:B⟶ℕ∪{−∞}\deg:B\longrightarrow\mathbb{N}\mathbb{\cup}\{-\infty\} such that, for all a,b∈Ba,b\in B, the following conditions are satisfied:

(1) deg⁡(a)=−∞\deg(a)=-\infty ⇔\Leftrightarrow a=0a=0.

(2) deg⁡(a​b)=deg⁡(a)+deg⁡(b)\deg(ab)=\deg(a)+\deg(b).

(3) deg⁡(a+b)≤m​a​x​{deg⁡(a),deg⁡(b)}\deg(a+b)\leq max\{\deg(a),\deg(b)\}.

If the equality in (2) replaced by the inequality deg⁡(a​b)≤deg⁡(a)+deg⁡(b)\deg(ab)\leq\deg(a)+\deg(b), we say that deg\deg is an ℕ\mathbb{N}-semi-degree function.

Indeed, for an ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function on BB, the sub-sets ℱi={b∈B∣deg⁡(b)≤i}\mathcal{F}_{i}=\{b\in B\mid\deg(b)\leq i\} are kk-subvector spaces of BB that give rise to a proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}. Conversely, every proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}, yields an ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function ω:B⟶ℕ∪{−∞}\omega:B\longrightarrow\mathbb{N}\mathbb{\cup}\{-\infty\} defined by ω⁡(0)=−∞\omega(0)=-\infty and ω⁡(b)=i\omega(b)=i if b∈ℱi∖ℱi−1b\in\mathcal{F}_{i}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{i-1}.

Definition 1.3.

Given a kk-domain B=∪i∈ℕℱiB=\cup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i} equipped with a proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration, the associated graded algebra Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{Gr}(B) is the kk-vector space

Gr(B)=⊕i∈ℕℱi/ℱi−1\mathrm{Gr}(B)=\oplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1}

equipped with the unique multiplicative structure for which the product of the elements a+ℱi−1∈ℱi/ℱi−1a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1}\in\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1} and b+ℱj−1∈ℱj/ℱj−1b+\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\in\mathcal{F}_{j}/\mathcal{F}_{j-1}, where a∈ℱia\in\mathcal{F}_{i} and b∈ℱjb\in\mathcal{F}_{j}, is the element

(a+ℱi−1)​(b+ℱj−1):=a​b+ℱi+j−1∈ℱi+j/ℱi+j−1.(a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})(b+\mathcal{F}_{j-1}):=ab+\mathcal{F}_{i+j-1}\in\mathcal{F}_{i+j}/\mathcal{F}_{i+j-1}.

Property 4 (proper) in Definition 1.1 ensures that Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{Gr}(B) is a commutative kk-domain when BB is an integral domain. Since for each a∈Ba\in B the set {n∈ℕ∣a∈ℱn}\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid a\in\mathcal{F}_{n}\} has a minimum, there exists ii such that a∈ℱia\in\mathcal{F}_{i} and a∉ℱi−1a\notin\mathcal{F}_{i-1}. So we can define a kk-linear map gr:B⟶Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{gr}:B\longrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}(B) by sending aa to its class in ℱi/ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1}, i.e a↦a+ℱi−1a\mapsto a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1}, and gr⁡(0)=0\mathrm{gr}(0)=0. We will frequently denote gr⁡(a)\mathrm{gr}(a) simply by a¯\overline{a}. Observe that gr⁡(a)=0\mathrm{gr}(a)=0 if and only if a=0a=0.

Denote by deg\deg the ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function deg:B⟶ℕ∪{−∞}\deg:B\longrightarrow\mathbb{N}\cup\{-\infty\} corresponding to the proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}. We have the following properties.

Lemma 1.4.

Given a,b∈Ba,b\in B the following holds:

P1) a​b¯=a¯​b¯\overline{a\,b}=\overline{a}\,\overline{b}, i.e. gr\mathrm{gr} is a multiplicative map.

P2) If deg⁡(a)>deg⁡(b)\deg(a)>\deg(b), then a+b¯=a¯\overline{a+b}=\overline{a}.

P3) If deg⁡(a)=deg⁡(b)=deg⁡(a+b)\deg(a)=\deg(b)=\deg(a+b), then a+b¯=a¯+b¯\overline{a+b}=\overline{a}+\overline{b}.

P4) If deg⁡(a)=deg⁡(b)>deg⁡(a+b)\deg(a)=\deg(b)>\deg(a+b), then a¯+b¯=0\overline{a}+\overline{b}=0, in particular gr\mathrm{gr} is not an additive map in general.

Proof.

Let us assume that deg⁡(a)=i\deg(a)=i and deg⁡(b)=j\deg(b)=j. By definition, deg⁡(a​b)=i+j\deg(ab)=i+j means that a​b∈ℱi+jab\in\mathcal{F}_{i+j} and a​b∉ℱi+j−1ab\notin\mathcal{F}_{i+j-1}, so a​b¯=a​b+ℱi+j−1:=(a+ℱi−1)​(b+ℱj−1)=a¯​b¯\overline{ab}=ab+\mathcal{F}_{i+j-1}:=(a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})(b+\mathcal{F}_{j-1})=\overline{a}\,\overline{b}. Which gives P1. For P2 we observe that since deg⁡(a+b)=deg⁡(a)\deg(a+b)=\deg(a), we have a+b¯=(a+b)+ℱi−1=(a+ℱi−1)+(b+ℱi−1)\overline{a+b}=(a+b)+\mathcal{F}_{i-1}=(a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})+(b+\mathcal{F}_{i-1}), and since ℱj−1⊂ℱj⊆ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\subset\mathcal{F}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{i-1} as i>ji>j, we get b+ℱi−1=0b+\mathcal{F}_{i-1}=0. P3) is immediate, by definition. Finally, assume by contradiction that a¯+b¯≠0\overline{a}+\overline{b}\neq 0, then a¯+b¯=(a+ℱi−1)+(b+ℱi−1)=((a+b)+ℱi−1)≠0\overline{a}+\overline{b}=(a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})+(b+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})=((a+b)+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})\neq 0, which means that a+b∉ℱi−1a+b\notin\mathcal{F}_{i-1} and deg⁡(a+b)=i\deg(a+b)=i, which is absurd. So P4 follows. ∎

1.2. Derivations


By a kk-derivation of BB, we mean a kk-linear map D:B⟶BD:B\longrightarrow B which satisfies the Leibniz rule: For all a,b∈Ba,b\in B; D⁡(a​b)=a​D​(b)+b​D​(a)D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a). The set of all kk-derivations of BB is denoted by Derk​(B)\mathrm{Der}_{k}(B).

The kernel of a derivation DD is the subalgebra ker⁡D={b∈B;D⁡(b)=0}\ker D=\left\{b\in B;D(b)=0\right\} of BB.

The plinth ideal of DD is the ideal pl⁡(D)=ker⁡D∩D⁡(B)\mathrm{pl}(D)=\ker D\cap D(B) of ker⁡D\mathrm{\ker}D, where D⁡(B)D(B) denotes the image of BB.

An element s∈Bs\in B such that D⁡(s)∈ker⁡(D)∖{0}D(s)\in\ker(D)\setminus\{0\} is called a local slice for DD.

Definition 1.5.

Given a kk-algebra B=∪i∈ℕℱiB=\cup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i} equipped with a proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration, a kk-derivation DD of BB is said to respect the filtration if there exists an integer dd such that D⁡(ℱi)⊂ℱi+dD(\mathcal{F}_{i})\subset\mathcal{F}_{i+d} for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

If so, we define a kk-linear map D¯:Gr⁡(B)⟶Gr⁡(B)\overline{D}:\mathrm{Gr}(B)\longrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}(B) as follows: If D=0D=0, then D¯=0\overline{D}=0 the zero map. Otherwise, if D≠0D\neq 0 then we let dd be the least integer such that D⁡(ℱi)⊂ℱi+dD(\mathcal{F}_{i})\subset\mathcal{F}_{i+d} for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} and we define

D¯:ℱi/ℱi−1⟶ℱi+d/ℱi+d−1\overline{D}:\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1}\longrightarrow\mathcal{F}_{i+d}/\mathcal{F}_{i+d-1}

by the rule D¯​(a+ℱi−1)=D⁡(a)+ℱi+d−1\overline{D}(a+\mathcal{F}_{i-1})=D(a)+\mathcal{F}_{i+d-1}. One checks that D¯\overline{D} satisfies the Leibniz rule, therefore it is a kk-derivation of the graded algebra Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{Gr}(B). Moreover it is homogeneous of degree dd, i.e D¯\overline{D} sends homogeneous elements of degree ii to zero or to homogeneous elements of degree i+di+d .

Observe that D¯=0\overline{D}=0 if and only if D=0D=0. In addition, gr⁡(ker⁡D)⊂ker⁡D¯\mathrm{gr}(\ker D)\subset\ker\overline{D}.

2. LND\mathrm{LND}-Filtrations and Associated Graded Algebras

In this section we introduce the ∂\partial-filtration associated with a locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial. We explain how to compute this filtration and its associated graded algebra in certain situation.

Definition 2.1.

A kk-derivation ∂∈Derk​(B)\partial\in\mathrm{Der}_{k}(B) is said to be locally nilpotent if for every a∈Ba\in B, there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} (depending of aa) such that ∂n(a)=0\partial^{n}(a)=0. The set of all locally nilpotent derivations of BB is denoted by LND⁡(B)\mathrm{\mathrm{LND}}(B).

In particular, every locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of BB gives rise to a proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration of BB by the sub-spaces ℱi=ker∂i\mathcal{F}_{i}=\mathrm{\ker}\partial^{i}, i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, that we call the ∂\partial-filtration. It is straightforward to check (see Prop. 1.9 in [1]) that the ∂\partial-filtration corresponds to the ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function deg∂:B⟶ℕ∪{−∞}\deg_{\partial}:B\longrightarrow\mathbb{N}\cup\{-\infty\} defined by

deg∂⁡(a):=m​i​n​{i∈ℕ∣∂i+1(a)=0}\deg_{\partial}(a):=min\{i\in\mathbb{N}\mid\partial^{i+1}(a)=0\}, and deg∂⁡(0):=−∞\deg_{\partial}(0):=-\infty.

Note that by definition ℱ0=ker∂\mathcal{F}_{0}=\ker\partial and that ℱ1∖ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{0} consists of all local slices for ∂\partial.
Let Gr∂(B)=⊕i∈ℕℱi/ℱi−1\mathrm{Gr}_{\partial}(B)=\oplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1} denote the associated graded algebra relative to the ∂\partial-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}. Let gr∂:B⟶Gr∂​(B)\mathrm{gr}_{\partial}:B\longrightarrow\mathrm{Gr_{\partial}}(B); a​⟼gr∂​a¯a\overset{\mathrm{gr}_{\partial}}{\longmapsto}\overline{a} be the natural map between BB and Gr∂​(B)\mathrm{Gr_{\partial}}(B) defined in 1.3, where a¯\overline{a} denote gr∂​(a)\mathrm{gr}_{\partial}(a).

The next Proposition, which is due to Daigle (Theorem 2.11 in [1]), implies in particular that if BB is of finite transcendence degree over kk, then every non-zero D∈LND⁡(B)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B) respects the ∂\partial-filtration and therefore induces a non-zero homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation D¯\overline{D} of Gr∂​(B)\mathrm{Gr}_{\partial}(B).

Proposition 2.2.

((Daigle)) Suppose that BB is a commutative domain, of finite transcendence degree over kk. Then for every pair D∈Derk​(B)D\in\mathrm{Der}_{k}(B) and ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{\mathrm{LND}}(B), DD respects the ∂\partial-filtration. Consequently, D¯\overline{D} is a well defined homogeneous derivation of the integral domain Gr∂​(B)\mathrm{Gr}_{\partial}(B) relative to this filtration, and it is locally nilpotent if DD is locally nilpotent.

2.1. Computing the ∂\partial-filtration


Here, given a finitely generated kk-domain BB, we describe a general method which enables the computation of the ∂\partial-filtration for a locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial with finitely generated kernel. First we consider a more general situation where the plinth ideal pl⁡(∂)\mathrm{pl}(\partial) is finitely generated as an ideal in ker∂\ker\partial then we deal with the case where ker∂\ker\partial is itself finitely generated as a kk-algebra.

Let B=k⁡[X1,…,Xn]/I=k⁡[x1,…,xn]B=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]/I=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be a finitely generated kk-domain, and let ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) be such that pl⁡(∂)\mathrm{pl}(\partial) is generated by precisely mm elements f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} as an ideal in ker∂\ker\partial. Lemma 2.3.

The filtrations ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are equal if and only if 𝒢\mathcal{G} is proper.

Proof.

B=k⁡[Z1,…,Zr]​[X1,…,Xn]​[S1,…,Sm]/J.B=k[Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{r}][X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}][S_{1},\ldots,S_{m}]/J.

Note that by construction (0,…,0)r+n+m​times∈Spec⁡(k[r+n+m]/J)\underset{r+n+m\mathrm{\,times}}{(0,\ldots,0)}\in\mathrm{Spec}(k^{[r+n+m]}/J).

We define an ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function ω\omega on k[r+n+m]k^{[r+n+m]} by declaring that ω⁡(Zi)=0=deg∂⁡(zi)\omega(Z_{i})=0=\deg_{\partial}(z_{i}) for all i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}, ω⁡(Si)=1=deg∂⁡(si)\omega(S_{i})=1=\deg_{\partial}(s_{i}) for all i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, and ω⁡(Xi)=deg∂⁡(xi)=di\omega(X_{i})=\deg_{\partial}(x_{i})=d_{i} for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. The corresponding proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration 𝒬i:={P∈k[n]∣ω⁡(P)≤i}\mathcal{Q}_{i}:=\{P\in k^{[n]}\mid\omega(P)\leq i\}, i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, on k[r+n+m]k^{[r+n+m]} has the form 𝒬i=⊕j≤iℋj\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}=\oplus_{j\leq i}\mathcal{H}_{j} where

ℋj:=⊕∑juj+∑idi​vi=jk[Z1,…,Zr]S1u1…SmumX1v1…Xnvn.\mathcal{H}_{j}:=\oplus_{\sum_{j}u_{j}+\sum_{i}d_{i}v_{i}=j}k[Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{r}]S_{1}^{u_{1}}\ldots S_{m}^{u_{m}}X_{1}^{v_{1}}\ldots X_{n}^{v_{n}}.

By construction π⁡(𝒬i)=𝒢i\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right)=\mathcal{G}_{i} where π:k[r+n+m]⟶B\pi:k^{[r+n+m]}\longrightarrow B denotes the natural projection. Indeed, since

π⁡(𝒬i)=∑j≤iπ⁡(ℋj)\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right)=\sum_{j\leq i}\pi\left(\mathcal{H}_{j}\right)

and π⁡(ℋj)=∑∑juj+∑idi​vi=jk⁡[z1,…,zr]​s1u1​….smum​x1v1​…​xnvn\pi\left(\mathcal{H}_{j}\right)=\sum_{\sum_{j}u_{j}+\sum_{i}d_{i}v_{i}=j}k[z_{1},\ldots,z_{r}]s_{1}^{u_{1}}\ldots.s_{m}^{u_{m}}x_{1}^{v_{1}}\ldots x_{n}^{v_{n}}, we get

π(ℋj)=∑∑juj+∑idi​vi=j(ker∂)s1u1.…smumx1v1.…xnvn\pi\left(\mathcal{H}_{j}\right)=\sum_{\sum_{j}u_{j}+\sum_{i}d_{i}v_{i}=j}\left(\ker\partial\right)s_{1}^{u_{1}}.\ldots s_{m}^{u_{m}}x_{1}^{v_{1}}.\ldots x_{n}^{v_{n}}

which means precisely that π⁡(𝒬i)=𝒢i\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right)=\mathcal{G}_{i}.

Let J^⊂k[r+n+m]\hat{J}\subset k^{[r+n+m]} be the homogeneous ideal generated by the highest homogeneous components relative to ω\omega of all elements in JJ. Then we have the following result, which is inspired by the technique developed by S. Kaliman and L. Makar-Limanov:

Proposition 2.4.

The ℕ\mathbb{N}-filration 𝒢\mathcal{G} is proper if and only if J^\hat{J} is prime.

Proof.

It is enough to show that 𝒢={π⁡(𝒬i)}i∈ℕ\mathcal{G}=\{\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right)\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} coincides with the filtration corresponding to the ℕ\mathbb{N}-semi-degree function ωB\omega_{B} on BB defined by ωB​(p):=minP∈π−1​(p)⁡{ω⁡(P)}\omega_{B}(p):=\min_{P\in\pi^{-1}(p)}\{\omega(P)\}. Indeed, if so, the result will follow from Lemma 3.2 in [5] which asserts in particular that ωB\omega_{B} is an ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function on BB if and only if J^\hat{J} is prime. Let {𝒢i′}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{G}_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} be the filtration corresponding to ωB\omega_{B}. Given f∈𝒢i′f\in\mathcal{G}_{i}^{{}^{\prime}} there exists F∈𝒬iF\in\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i} such that π⁡(F)=f\pi(F)=f, which means that 𝒢i′⊂π(𝒬i)\mathcal{G}_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\subset\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right). Conversely, it is clear that ωB​(zi)=ω⁡(Zi)=0\omega_{B}(z_{i})=\omega(Z_{i})=0 for all i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}. Furthermore ωB​(si)=ω⁡(Si)=1\omega_{B}(s_{i})=\omega(S_{i})=1 for all i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, for otherwise si∈ker∂s_{i}\in\ker\partial which is absurd. Finally, if di≠0d_{i}\neq 0 and ωB​(xi)<ω⁡(Xi)=di≠0\omega_{B}(x_{i})<\omega(X_{i})=d_{i}\neq 0, then xi∈π(𝒬di−1)⊂ker∂di−1x_{i}\in\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{d_{i}-1}\right)\subset\ker\partial^{d_{i}-1} which implies that deg∂⁡(xi)<di\deg_{\partial}(x_{i})<d_{i}, a contradiction. So ωB​(xi)=di\omega_{B}(x_{i})=d_{i}. Thus ωB​(f)≤i\omega_{B}(f)\leq i for every f∈π⁡(𝒬i)f\in\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right) which means that π(𝒬i)⊂𝒢i′\pi\left(\mathcal{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\right)\subset\mathcal{G}_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}. ∎

The next Proposition, which is a reinterpretation of Prop. 4.1 in [5], describes in particular the associated graded algebra G​r∂​(B)Gr_{\partial}(B) of the filtered algebra (B,ℱ)\left(B,\mathcal{F}\right) in the case where the ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration 𝒢\mathcal{G} is proper:

Proposition 2.5.

If the ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration 𝒢\mathcal{G} is proper then G​r∂​(B)≃k[r+n+m]/J^Gr_{\partial}(B)\simeq k^{[r+n+m]}/\hat{J}.

Proof.

By virtue of (( Prop. 4.1 in [5])) the graded algebra associated to the filtered algebra (B,𝒢)\left(B,\mathcal{G}\right) is isomorphic to k[r+n+m]/J^k^{[r+n+m]}/\hat{J}. So the assertion follows from Lemma 2.3. ∎

3. Semi-Rigid and Rigid kk-Domains

In [7] D. Finston and S. Maubach considered rings BB whose sets of locally nilpotent derivations are “one-dimensional” in the sense that LND⁡(B)=ker⁡(∂).∂\mathrm{LND}(B)=\ker(\partial).\partial for some non-zero ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B). They called them almost-rigid rings. Hereafter, we consider the following definition which seems more natural in our context (see Prop. 3.2 below for a comparison between the two notions).

Definition 3.1.

A commutative domain BB over a field kk of characteristic zero is called semi-rigid if all non-zero locally nilpotent derivations of BB induce the same proper ℕ\mathbb{N}-filtration (equivalently, the same ℕ\mathbb{N}-degree function).

Recall that the Makar-Limanov invariant of a commutative kk-domain BB over a field kk of characteristic zero is defined by

ML(B):=∩D∈LND⁡(B)ker(D).\mathrm{ML}(B):=\cap_{D\in\mathrm{\mathrm{LND}}(B)}\ker(D).

In particular, BB is semi-rigid if and only if ML⁡(B)=ker⁡(∂)\mathrm{ML}(B)=\ker(\partial) for any non-zero ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B). Indeed, given D,E∈LND⁡(B)∖{0}D,E\in\mathrm{LND}(B)\setminus\{0\} such that A:=ker⁡(D)=ker⁡(E)A:=\ker(D)=\ker(E), there exist non-zero elements a,b∈Aa,b\in A such that a​D=b​EaD=bE (see [1] Principle 12) which implies that the DD-filtration is equal to the EE-filtration. So if ML⁡(B)=ker⁡(∂)\mathrm{ML}(B)=\ker(\partial) for any non-zero ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) then BB is semi-rigid. The other implication is clear by definition.

Recall that D∈Derk​(B)D\in\mathrm{Der}_{k}(B) is irreducible if and only if D⁡(B)D(B) is contained in no proper principal ideal of BB, and that BB is said to satisfy the ascending chain condition (ACC) on principal ideals if and only if every infinite chain (b1)⊂(b2)⊂(b3)⊂⋯(b_{1})\subset(b_{2})\subset(b_{3})\subset\cdots of principal ideals of BB eventually stabilizes. BB is said to be a highest common factor ring, or HCF-ring, if and only if the intersection of any two principal ideals of BB is again principal.

Proposition 3.2.

Let BB be a semi-rigid kk-domain satisfying the ACC on principal ideals. If ML⁡(B)\mathrm{ML}(B) is an HCF-ring, then there exists a unique irreducible ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) up to multiplication by unit.

Proof.

Existence: since BB is satisfies the ACC on principal ideals, then for every non-zero T∈LND⁡(B)T\in\mathrm{LND}(B), there exists an irreducible T0∈LND⁡(B)T_{0}\in\mathrm{LND}(B) and c∈ker⁡(T)c\in\ker(T) such that T=c​T0T=cT_{0}. (see [1], Prop. 2.2 and Principle 7).

Uniqueness: the following argument is similar to that in [1] Prop. 2.2.b, but with a little difference, that is, in [1] it is assumed that BB itself is an HCF-ring while here we only require that ML⁡(B)\mathrm{ML}(B) is an HCF-ring.

Let D,E∈LND⁡(B)D,E\in\mathrm{LND}(B) be irreducible derivations, and denote A=ML⁡(B)A=\mathrm{ML}(B). By hypothesis ker⁡(D)=ker⁡(E)=A\ker(D)=\ker(E)=A, so there exist non-zero a,b∈Aa,b\in A such that a​D=b​EaD=bE (see [1] Principle 12). Here we can assume that a,ba,b are not units otherwise we are done. Set T=a​D=b​ET=aD=bE. Since AA is an HCF-ring, there exists c∈Ac\in A such that a​A∩b​A=c​AaA\cap bA=cA. Therefore, T⁡(B)⊂c​BT(B)\subset cB, and there exists T0∈LND⁡(B)T_{0}\in\mathrm{LND}(B) such that T=c​T0T=cT_{0}. Write c=a​s=b​tc=as=bt for s,t∈Bs,t\in B. Then c​T0=a​s​T0=a​DcT_{0}=asT_{0}=aD implies D=s​T0D=sT_{0}, and likewise E=t​T0E=tT_{0}. By irreducibility, ss and tt are units of BB, and we are done. ∎

In particular, for a ring BB as in 3.2, every D∈LND⁡(B)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B) has the form D=f∂D=f\partial for some irreducible ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) and f∈ker⁡(∂)f\in\ker(\partial), and so BB is almost rigid in the sense introduced by Finston and Maubach.

Recall that a ring AA is called rigid if the zero derivation is the only locally nilpotent derivation of AA. Equivalently, AA is rigid if and only if ML⁡(A)=A\mathrm{ML}(A)=A. It is well known that the only non rigid kk-domains of transcendence degree one are polynomial rings in one variable over algebraic extensions of kk ([1] Corollary 1.24 and Corollary 1.29). In particular, we have the following elementary criterion for rigidity that we will use frequently in the sequel:

Lemma 3.3.

A domain BB of transcendence degree one over a field kk of characteristic zero is rigid if one of the following properties hold:

(1) BB is not factorial.

(2) Spec⁡(B)\mathrm{Spec}(B) has a singular point.

3.1. Elementary examples of semi-rigid kk-domains


The next Proposition, which is due to Makar-Limanov ([8] Lemma 21, also [9] Theorem 3.1), presents some of the simplest examples of semi-rigid kk-domains.

Proposition 3.4.

((Makar-Limanov)) Let AA be a rigid domain of finite transcendence degree over a field kk of characteristic zero. Then the polynomial ring A⁡[x]A[x] is semi-rigid.

Proof.

For the convenience of the reader, we provide an argument formulated in the LND\mathrm{LND}-filtration language. Let ∂\partial be the locally nilpotent derivation of A⁡[x]A[x] defined by ∂(a)=0\partial(a)=0 for every a∈Aa\in A and ∂(x)=1\partial(x)=1. Then the ∂\partial-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} is given by ℱi=A​xi⊕ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i}=Ax^{i}\oplus\mathcal{F}_{i-1} where ℱ0=ker⁡(∂)=A\mathcal{F}_{0}=\ker(\partial)=A. So the associated graded algebra is Gr(A[x])=⊕i∈ℕAx¯iGr(A[x])=\oplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}A\overline{x}^{i}, where x¯:=g​r​(x)\overline{x}:=gr(x). By Proposition 2.2, every non-zero D∈LND⁡(A⁡[x])D\in\mathrm{LND}(A[x]) respects the ∂\partial-filtration and induces a non-zero homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation D¯\overline{D} of Gr⁡(A⁡[x])\mathrm{Gr}(A[x]) of a certain degree dd.

Let f∈ker⁡(D)f\in\ker(D) and assume that f∉Af\notin A. Then x¯\overline{x} divides f¯\overline{f}. Since f¯∈ker⁡(D¯)\overline{f}\in\ker(\overline{D}) and ker⁡(D¯)\ker(\overline{D}) is factorially closed ([1] Principle 1), we have x¯∈ker⁡(D¯)\overline{x}\in\ker(\overline{D}). Note that D¯\overline{D} sends homogeneous elements of degree ii to zero or to homogeneous elements of degree i+di+d, therefore D¯\overline{D} has the form D¯=a​x¯d​E\overline{D}=a\overline{x}^{d}E, where a∈Aa\in A, d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, and E∈LND⁡(A)E\in\mathrm{LND}(A) see [1] Principle 7. But since AA is rigid, E=0E=0. Thus D¯=0\overline{D}=0, a contradiction. This means f∈Af\in A which implies that ker⁡(D)⊂A\ker(D)\subset A. Finally, since tr.degk​(A)=tr.degk​(ker⁡(D))\mathrm{tr.deg_{k}}(A)=\mathrm{tr.deg_{k}}(\ker(D)) and AA is algebraically closed in A⁡[x]A[x], we get the equality ker⁡(D)=A\ker(D)=A. Hence ML⁡(A⁡[x])=A\mathrm{ML}(A[x])=A. ∎

4. Computing the ML\mathrm{ML}-Invariant using LND\mathrm{LND}-Filtration

Here we illustrate the use of the ∂\partial-filtration in the computation of ML\mathrm{ML}-invariants, for classes of already well-studied examples.

4.1. Classical examples of semi-rigid kk-domains


We first consider in 4.1.1, certain surfaces in 𝔸[3]\mathbb{A}^{[3]} defined by equations Xn​Z−P⁡(Y)X^{n}Z-P(Y) where n>1n>1 and degY⁡P⁡(Y)>1\deg_{Y}P(Y)>1, which were first discussed by Makar-Limanov in [8], where he computed their ML\mathrm{ML}-invariants. Later on Poloni [11] used similar methods to compute ML\mathrm{ML}-invariants for a larger class. In the second example 4.1.2, we consider certain threefolds whose invariants were computed by S. Kaliman and L. Makar-Limanov [6] in the context of the linearization problem for ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action on ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3}.

In these examples, the use of LND\mathrm{LND}-filtrations is more natural and less tedious than other existing approaches.

4.1.1. Danielewski hypersurfaces


Let

Bn,P=k⁡[X,Y,Z]/⟨Xn​Z−P⁡(X,Y)⟩B_{n,P}=k[X,Y,Z]/\langle X^{n}Z-P(X,Y)\rangle

where

P⁡(X,Y)=Ym+fm−1​(X)​Ym−1+⋯+f0​(X),P(X,Y)=Y^{m}+f_{m-1}(X)Y^{m-1}+\cdots+f_{0}(X),

fi​(X)∈k​[X]f_{i}(X)\in k[X], n≥2n\geq 2, and m≥2m\geq 2.

Let xx, yy, zz be the images of XX, YY, ZZ in Bn,PB_{n,P}. Define ∂\partial by ∂(x)=0\partial(x)=0, ∂(y)=xn\partial(y)=x^{n}, ∂(z)=∂P∂y\partial(z)=\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} where

∂P∂y=m​ym−1+(m−1)​fm−1​(x)​ym−2+…+f1​(x)\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=my^{m-1}+(m-1)f_{m-1}(x)y^{m-2}+\ldots+f_{1}(x)

We see that ∂∈LND⁡(Bn,P)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B_{n,P}) with ker⁡(∂)=k⁡[x]\ker(\partial)=k[x], and yy is a local slice for ∂\partial. Moreover, we have deg∂⁡(x)=0\deg_{\partial}(x)=0, deg∂⁡(y)=1\deg_{\partial}(y)=1, deg∂⁡(z)=m\deg_{\partial}(z)=m. The plinth ideal is pl⁡(∂)=⟨xn⟩\mathrm{pl}(\partial)=\left\langle x^{n}\right\rangle. Up to a change of variable of the form Y↦Y−cY\mapsto Y-c where c∈kc\in k, we can always assume that 0∈Spec⁡(B)0\in\mathrm{Spec}(B). A consequence of Lemma 2.3, Proposition 2.4, and Proposition 2.5 (see the Proof of Prop. 5.1 for more details) is that

1- The ∂\partial-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} is given by:

ℱm​i+j=k⁡[x]​yj​zi+ℱm​i+j−1\mathcal{F}_{mi+j}=k[x]y^{j}z^{i}+\mathcal{F}_{mi+j-1}

where i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} and j∈{0,…​m−1}j\in\{0,\ldots m-1\}.

2- The associated graded algebra Gr(Bn,P)=⊕i∈ℕB¯i\mathrm{Gr}(B_{n,P})=\oplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{B}_{i}, where B¯i=ℱi/ℱi−1\overline{B}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{i}/\mathcal{F}_{i-1}, is generated by x¯=g​r∂​(x)\overline{x}=gr_{\partial}(x), y¯=g​r∂​(y)\overline{y}=gr_{\partial}(y), z¯=g​r∂​(z)\overline{z}=gr_{\partial}(z) as an algebra over kk with relation x¯n​z¯=y¯m\overline{x}^{n}\overline{z}=\overline{y}^{m}, i.e. Gr⁡(Bn,P)=k⁡[X¯,Y¯,Z¯]/⟨X¯n​Z¯−Y¯m⟩\mathrm{Gr}(B_{n,P})=k[\overline{X},\overline{Y},\overline{Z}]/\langle\overline{X}^{n}\overline{Z}-\overline{Y}^{m}\rangle. And we have :

B¯m​i+j=k⁡[x¯]​y¯j​z¯i\overline{B}_{mi+j}=k[\overline{x}]\overline{y}^{j}\overline{z}^{i}

where i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} and j∈{0,…​m−1}j\in\{0,\ldots m-1\}.

Proposition 4.1.

With the notation above we have:

(1) ML⁡(Bn,P)=k⁡[x]\mathrm{ML}(B_{n,P})=k[x]. Consequently Bn,PB_{n,P} is semi-rigid.

(2) Every D∈LND⁡(Bn,P)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B_{n,P}) has the form D=f(x)∂D=f(x)\partial.

Proof.

(1) By Proposition 2.2 a non-zero D∈LND⁡(B)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B) induces a non-zero D¯∈LND⁡(Gr⁡(B))\overline{D}\in\mathrm{LND}\left(\mathrm{Gr}(B)\right). Let f∈ker⁡(D)∖kf\in\ker(D)\setminus k, then f¯∈ker⁡(D¯)∖k\overline{f}\in\ker(\overline{D})\setminus k. There exists i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} such that f¯∈B¯i\overline{f}\in\overline{B}_{i}.

Assume that f¯∉k⁡[x¯]=B¯0\overline{f}\notin k[\overline{x}]=\overline{B}_{0}, then one of the elements y¯,z¯\overline{y},\overline{z} must divide f¯\overline{f} . Which leads to a contradiction as follows:

If y¯\overline{y} divides f¯\overline{f} , then y¯∈ker⁡(D¯)\overline{y}\in\ker(\overline{D}) because ker⁡(D¯)\ker(\overline{D}) is factorially closed in Gr⁡(B)\mathrm{Gr}(B) ([1] Principle 1). For the same reason x¯,z¯∈ker⁡(D¯)\overline{x},\overline{z}\in\ker(\overline{D}) because x¯n​z¯=y¯m\overline{x}^{n}\overline{z}=\overline{y}^{m}. So D¯=0\overline{D}=0, a contradiction.

If z¯\overline{z} divides f¯\overline{f}, then D¯​(z¯)=0\overline{D}(\overline{z})=0. So D¯\overline{D} extends to a locally nilpotent derivation D~\widetilde{D} of the ring B~=k⁡(z¯)​[x¯,y¯]/⟨x¯n​z¯−y¯m⟩\widetilde{B}=k(\overline{z})[\overline{x},\overline{y}]/\left\langle\overline{x}^{n}\overline{z}-\overline{y}^{m}\right\rangle. Since 0∈Spec⁡(B)0\in\mathrm{Spec}(B) is a singular point when n≥2n\geq 2 and m≥2m\geq 2 , B~\widetilde{B} is rigid (Lemma 3.3). Therefore, D~=0\widetilde{D}=0 which means D¯=0\overline{D}=0, a contradiction.

So the only possibility is that f¯∈k⁡[x¯]\overline{f}\in k[\overline{x}]. This means that deg∂⁡(f)=0\deg_{\partial}(f)=0, and hence that f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x]. So ker⁡(D)⊂k⁡[x]\ker(D)\subset k[x], and finally k⁡[x]=ker⁡(D)k[x]=\ker(D) because tr.degk​(ker⁡(D))=1\mathrm{tr.deg_{k}}(\ker(D))=1 and k⁡[x]k[x] is algebraically closed in BB. So we get ML⁡(B)=k⁡[x]\mathrm{ML}(B)=k[x].

(2) is an immediate consequence of Proposition 3.2. ∎

4.1.2. Koras-Russell hypersurfaces of the second type


Here we consider hypersurfaces associated with kk-algebras of the form:

Bn,e,l,Q=k[X,Y,Z,T]/⟨Y(Xn+Ze)l−Q(X,Z,T⟩B_{n,e,l,Q}=k[X,Y,Z,T]/\langle Y(X^{n}+Z^{e})^{l}-Q(X,Z,T\rangle

where

Q⁡(X,Z,T)=Tm+f1​(X,Z)​Tm−1+…+fm​(X,Z)Q(X,Z,T)=T^{m}+f_{1}(X,Z)T^{m-1}+\ldots+f_{m}(X,Z)

fi​(X,Z)∈k⁡[X,Z]f_{i}(X,Z)\in k[X,Z], n>1n>1, e>1e>1, l>1l>1, and m>1m>1. We may assume without loss of generality that Q⁡(0,0,0)=0Q(0,0,0)=0 . A particular case of this family corresponds to the so called Koras-Russell hypersurfaces of the second type considered by S. Kaliman and L. Makar-Limanov ([6]) where they computed their ML\mathrm{ML}-invariants. Here we explain how to apply the LND\mathrm{LND}-filtration method to compute this invariant for all algebras Bn,e,l,QB_{n,e,l,Q}.

Let xx, yy, zz, tt be the images of XX, YY, ZZ, TT in Bn,e,l,QB_{n,e,l,Q}. Define ∂\partial by

∂=∂Q∂t∂y+(Xn+Ze)l∂t\partial=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t}\partial_{y}+(X^{n}+Z^{e})^{l}\partial_{t}

We see that ∂∈LND⁡(Bn,e,l,Q)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B_{n,e,l,Q}) with ker⁡(∂)=k⁡[x,z]\ker(\partial)=k[x,z], and tt is a local slice for ∂\partial. Moreover, we have deg∂⁡(x)=0\deg_{\partial}(x)=0, deg∂⁡(y)=m\deg_{\partial}(y)=m, deg∂⁡(z)=0\deg_{\partial}(z)=0, and deg∂⁡(t)=1\deg_{\partial}(t)=1. The plinth ideal is pl⁡(∂)=⟨(Xn+Ze)l⟩\mathrm{pl}(\partial)=\langle(X^{n}+Z^{e})^{l}\rangle. By Lemma 2.3, Prop. 2.4, and Prop. 2.5 we get the following.

1- The ∂\partial-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} is given by:

ℱm​i+j=k⁡[x,z]​tj​yi+ℱm​i+j−1\mathcal{F}_{mi+j}=k[x,z]t^{j}y^{i}+\mathcal{F}_{mi+j-1}

where i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, and j∈{0,…,m−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}.

With the notation above we have:

5. A new class of semi-rigid rings

In this section, we use the LND\mathrm{LND}-filtration method to establish the semi-rigidity of new families of two dimensional domains of the form

R=k⁡[X,Y,Z]/⟨Xn​Y−P⁡(X,Q⁡(X,Y)−Xe​Z)⟩R=k[X,Y,Z]/\left\langle X^{n}Y-P\left(X,Q(X,Y)-X^{e}Z\right)\right\rangle

for suitable integers n,e≥2n,e\geq 2 and polynomials P⁡(X,T),Q⁡(X,T)∈k⁡[X,T]P(X,T),Q(X,T)\in k[X,T]. They share with Danielewski hypersurfaces discussed in 4.1.1 above, the property to come naturally equipped with an irreducible locally nilpotent derivation induced by a locally nilpotent derivation of k⁡[X,Y,Z]k[X,Y,Z]. But in contrast with the Danielewski hypersurfaces case, the corresponding derivation on k⁡[X,Y,Z]k[X,Y,Z] are no longer triangular, in fact not even triangulable by virtue of characterization due to Daigle [10].

We will begin with a very elementary example illustrating the steps needed to determine the LND\mathrm{LND}-filtration and its associated graded algebra, and then we proceed to the general case.

5.1. A toy example


We let

R=k⁡[X,Y,Z]/⟨X2​Y−(Y2−X​Z)2⟩R=k[X,Y,Z]/\langle X^{2}Y-(Y^{2}-XZ)^{2}\rangle

of k⁡[X,Y,Z]k[X,Y,Z] where S:=Y2−X​ZS:=Y^{2}-XZ is locally nilpotent and annihilates the polynomial X2​Y−(Y2−X​Z)2X^{2}Y-(Y^{2}-XZ)^{2}. Furthermore, the element s=y2−x​zs=y^{2}-xz is a local slice for ∂\partial with ∂(s)=x3\partial(s)=x^{3}. The kernel of ∂\partial is k⁡[x]k[x] and the plinth ideal is the principal ideal generated by x3x^{3}. We have deg∂⁡(x)=0\deg_{\partial}(x)=0, deg∂⁡(y)=2\deg_{\partial}(y)=2, deg∂⁡(z)=4\deg_{\partial}(z)=4, deg∂⁡(s)=1\deg_{\partial}(s)=1.

5.2. A more general family


We now consider more generally rings RR of the form

ℱm​d​i+d​j+l=k⁡[x]​sl​yj​zi+ℱm​d​i+d​j+l−1\mathcal{F}_{mdi+dj+l}=k[x]s^{l}y^{j}z^{i}+\mathcal{F}_{mdi+dj+l-1}

Theorem 5.2.

With the above notation the following hold:

(1) ML⁡(R)=k⁡[x]\mathrm{ML}(R)=k[x]. Consequently RR is semi-rigid.

(1) Given a non-zero D∈LND⁡(R)D\in\mathrm{LND}(R). By Proposition 2.2, DD respects the ∂\partial-filtration and induces a non-zero locally nilpotent derivation D¯\overline{D} of Gr⁡(R)\mathrm{Gr}(R). Assume that f¯∉k⁡[x¯]=R¯0\overline{f}\notin k[\overline{x}]=\overline{R}_{0}, then one of the elements s¯\overline{s}, y¯\overline{y}, z¯\overline{z} must divides f¯\overline{f} by 5.2,2. Which leads to a contradiction as follows :

But since 0∈Spec⁡(R~)0\in\mathrm{Spec(\widetilde{R})} is a singular point, R~\widetilde{R} is rigid (Lemma 3.3). So D~=0\widetilde{D}=0, which implies D¯=0\overline{D}=0, a contradiction.

So the only possibility is that f¯∈k⁡[x¯]\overline{f}\in k[\overline{x}], and this means deg∂⁡(f)=0\deg_{\partial}(f)=0, thus f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] and ker⁡(D)⊂k⁡[x]\ker(D)\subset k[x]. Finally, k⁡[x]=ker⁡(D)k[x]=\ker(D) because tr.degk​(ker⁡(D))=1\mathrm{tr.deg_{k}}(\ker(D))=1 and k⁡[x]k[x] is algebraically closed in BB. So ML⁡(R)=k⁡[x]\mathrm{ML}(R)=k[x].

(2) follows again from Proposition 3.2. ∎

6. Further applications of the LND\mathrm{LND}-filtratoin

Given a commutative domain BB over an algebraically closed field kk of characteristic zero, we denote Autk​(B)\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B) the group of algebraic kk-automorphisms of BB. This group acts by conjugation on LND⁡(B)\mathrm{LND}(B). An immediate consequence is that α⁡(ML⁡(B))=ML⁡(B)\alpha(\mathrm{ML}(B))=\mathrm{ML}(B) for every α∈Autk​(B)\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B) which yield in particular an induced action of Autk​(B)\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B) on ML⁡(B)\mathrm{ML}(B). Let ∂α=α−1∂α\partial_{\alpha}=\alpha^{-1}\partial\alpha be the conjugate of ∂\partial by a given automorphism α\alpha of BB, it is straightforward to check that α{ker(∂α)}=ker(∂)\alpha\{\ker(\partial_{\alpha})\}=\ker(\partial) and more generally that deg∂α⁡(b)=deg∂⁡(α⁡(b))\deg_{\partial_{\alpha}}(b)=\deg_{\partial}(\alpha(b)) for any b∈Bb\in B. In other words, α\alpha respects deg∂\deg_{\partial} and deg∂α\deg_{\partial_{\alpha}}(i.e. α\alpha sends an element of degree nn relative to deg∂α\deg_{\partial_{\alpha}}, to an element of the same degree nn relative to deg∂\deg_{\partial}.

Definition 6.1.

We say that an algebraic kk-automorphism α\alpha preserves the ∂\partial-filtration for some ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) if deg∂⁡(α⁡(b))=deg∂⁡(b)\deg_{\partial}(\alpha(b))=\deg_{\partial}(b) for any b∈Bb\in B.

Lemma 6.2.

Let ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) and α∈Autk​(B)\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B). Then ∂\partial and ∂α\partial_{\alpha} are equivalent, i.e. have the same kernel, if and only if α\alpha preserve the ∂\partial-filtration.

Proof.

Suppose that ∂\partial and ∂α\partial_{\alpha} are equivalents, then deg∂⁡(α⁡(b))=deg∂α⁡(b)\deg_{\partial}(\alpha(b))=\deg_{\partial_{\alpha}}(b) for every b∈Bb\in B, and by hypothesis ker(∂)=ker(∂α)\ker(\partial)=\ker(\partial_{\alpha}), so deg∂=deg∂α\deg_{\partial}=\deg_{\partial_{\alpha}}. Then we obtain deg∂⁡(α⁡(b))=deg∂⁡(b)\deg_{\partial}(\alpha(b))=\deg_{\partial}(b). Thus α\alpha preserves the ∂\partial-filtration. Since the other direction is obvious we are done. ∎

The following Corollary shows a nice property of a semi-rigid ring. That is, every algebraic automorphism α\alpha has to preserve the unique filtration induced by any locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial, i.e. α\alpha sends an element of degree ii relative to ∂\partial to an element of the same degree relative to ∂\partial. Which makes the computation of the group of automorphisms easier up to the automorphism group of ker⁡(∂)\ker(\partial).

Corollary 6.3.

Let BB be a semi-rigid kk-domain, then every kk-automorphism of BB preserve the ∂\partial-filtration for every ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B).

Proof.

A direct consequence of Definition 3.1 and Lemma 6.2. ∎

6.1. The group of algebraic kk-automorphisms of a semi-rigid kk-domain


Suppose that BB is a semi-rigid kk-domain. Then, it has a unique proper filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} which is the ∂\partial-filtration corresponding to any non-zero locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of BB. Since every algebraic kk-automorphism of BB preserves this filtration (Corollary 6.3), we obtain an exact sequence

0→Autk​(B,ML⁡(B))→Autk​(B)→Autk​(ML⁡(B))0\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut_{k}}\left(B,\mathrm{ML}(B)\right)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut_{k}}\left(\mathrm{ML}(B)\right)

where Autk​(B,ML​(B))\mathrm{Aut_{k}}\left(B,\mathrm{ML}(B)\right) is by definition the sub-group of Autk​(B)\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B) consisting of elements whose induced action on ML⁡(B)\mathrm{ML}(B) is trivial. Furthermore, every element of Autk​(B,ML​(B))\mathrm{Aut_{k}}\left(B,\mathrm{ML}(B)\right) induces for every i≥1i\geq 1 an automorphism of ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}-module of each ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}. In this section we illustrate how to exploit these information to compute Autk​(B)\mathrm{Aut_{k}}(B) for certain semi-rigid kk-domains BB.

6.1.1. Autk\mathrm{Aut_{k}} for example 4.1.1


In [8] Makar-Limanov computed the kk-automorphism group for surfaces in k[3]k^{[3]} defined by equation Xn​Z−P⁡(Y)=0X^{n}Z-P(Y)=0 where n>1n>1 and degY⁡P⁡(Y)>1\deg_{Y}P(Y)>1. Then Poloni, see [11], generalized Makar-Limanov’s method to obtained similar results for the rings considered in 4.1.1 above. Here we briefly indicate how to recover these results using LND\mathrm{LND}-filtrations. So let

Bn,P=k⁡[X,Y,Z]/⟨Xn​Z−P⁡(X,Y)⟩B_{n,P}=k[X,Y,Z]/\left\langle X^{n}Z-P(X,Y)\right\rangle

where P⁡(X,Y)=Ym+fm−1​(X)​Ym−1+⋯+f0​(X)P(X,Y)=Y^{m}+f_{m-1}(X)Y^{m-1}+\cdots+f_{0}(X), fi​(X)∈k​[X]f_{i}(X)\in k[X], n≥2n\geq 2, and m≥2m\geq 2. Up to change of variable of the form YY by Y−fm−1​(X)mY-\frac{f_{m-1}(X)}{m} we may assume without loss of generality that fm−1​(X)=0f_{m-1}(X)=0.

Proposition 6.4.

Let Bn,PB_{n,P} be as above. Then every algebraic kk-automorphism α\alpha of BB has the form

α⁡(x,y,z)=(λ​x,μ​y+xn​a​(x),μmλn​z+P⁡(λ​x,μ​y+xn​a​(x))−μm​P​(x,y)λn​xn)\alpha(x,y,z)=(\lambda x,\,\mu y+x^{n}a(x),\,\frac{\mu^{m}}{\lambda^{n}}z+\frac{P(\lambda x,\mu y+x^{n}a(x))-\mu^{m}P(x,y)}{\lambda^{n}x^{n}})

where λ,μ∈k∗\lambda,\mu\in k^{*} satisfy fm−i​(λ​x)≡μi.fm−i​(x)f_{m-i}(\lambda x)\equiv\mu^{i}.f_{m-i}(x) mod xnx^{n} for all ii, and a⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]a(x)\in k[x].

Proof.

By Proposition 4.1, (1) and §4.1.1, ML⁡(B)=k⁡[x]\mathrm{ML}(B)=k[x] and the ∂\partial-filtration {ℱi}i∈ℕ\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} is given by ℱi​m+j=k⁡[x]​yi​m+j+k⁡[x]​yi​m+j−m​z+…+k⁡[x]​yj​zi+ℱi​m+j−1\mathcal{F}_{im+j}=k[x]y^{im+j}+k[x]y^{im+j-m}z+\ldots+k[x]y^{j}z^{i}+\mathcal{F}_{im+j-1}, where ∂=xn.∂y+∂P∂y.∂z\partial=x^{n}.\partial_{y}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}.\partial_{z}, deg∂⁡(x)=0\deg_{\partial}(x)=0, deg∂⁡(y)=1\deg_{\partial}(y)=1, and deg∂⁡(z)=m\deg_{\partial}(z)=m. In particular ℱ0=k⁡[x]\mathcal{F}_{0}=k[x], ℱ1=k⁡[x]​y+ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{1}=k[x]y+\mathcal{F}_{0}, and ℱm=k⁡[x]​ym+k⁡[x]​z+ℱm−1\mathcal{F}_{m}=k[x]y^{m}+k[x]z+\mathcal{F}_{m-1}.

Now by Corollary 6.3 α\alpha preserve deg∂\deg_{\partial}, so we must have α⁡(x)∈ℱ0=k⁡[x]\alpha(x)\in\mathcal{F}_{0}=k[x], α⁡(y)∈ℱ1=k⁡[x]​y+k⁡[x]\alpha(y)\in\mathcal{F}_{1}=k[x]y+k[x] and α⁡(z)∈ℱm=k⁡[x]​ym+k⁡[x].z+ℱm−1\alpha(z)\in\mathcal{F}_{m}=k[x]y^{m}+k[x].z+\mathcal{F}_{m-1}. Since α\alpha is invertible we get α⁡(x)=λ​x+c\alpha(x)=\lambda x+c, α⁡(y)=μ​y+b⁡(x)\alpha(y)=\mu y+b(x), and α⁡(z)=ξ​z+h⁡(x,y)\alpha(z)=\xi z+h(x,y) where λ,μ,ξ∈k∗\lambda,\mu,\xi\in k^{*}, c∈kc\in k, b∈k⁡[x]b\in k[x], h⁡(x,y)∈k⁡[x,y]h(x,y)\in k[x,y], and degy⁡h⁡(x,y)≤m\deg_{y}h(x,y)\leq m.

By Proposition 4.1 (2) every D∈LND⁡(B)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B) has the form D=f(x)∂D=f(x)\partial. In particular, ∂α=f(x)∂\partial_{\alpha}=f(x)\partial for some f⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]f(x)\in k[x]. Since α∂α=∂α\alpha\partial_{\alpha}=\partial\alpha we have ∂(α⁡(y))=α⁡(f⁡(x)​∂(y))=f⁡(α⁡(x))​α​(xn)\partial(\alpha(y))=\alpha(f(x)\partial(y))=f(\alpha(x))\alpha(x^{n}) where (∂(y)=xn\partial(y)=x^{n}). So xnx^{n} divides −μi​fm−i​(x)+fm−i​(λ​x)-\mu^{i}f_{m-i}(x)+f_{m-i}(\lambda x) for every ii. And we are done. ∎

6.2. Isomorphisms


We are going to use the previous facts about semi-rigid kk-domains to give a necessary and sufficient condition for two hypersurfaces of the family 4.1.1 to be isomorphic.

Let Ψ:A⟶B\Psi:A\longrightarrow B be an algebraic isomorphism, we refer to this by Ψ∈Isom(A,B)k\Psi\in\mathrm{Isom}{}_{k}(A,B), between two finitely generated kk-domains A=k⁡[y1,…,yr]A=k[y_{1},\ldots,y_{r}], B=k⁡[x1,…,xr]B=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}] where y1,…,yry_{1},\ldots,y_{r} and x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r} are minimal sets of generators. Since Ψ⁡(A)=k⁡[Ψ⁡(y1),…,Ψ⁡(yr)]=k⁡[x1,…,xr]\Psi(A)=k[\Psi(y_{1}),\ldots,\Psi(y_{r})]=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}], there exists an automorphism ψ:B⟶B\psi:B\longrightarrow B such that for every i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\ldots,r\} there exists j∈{1,…,r}j\in\{1,\ldots,r\} such that ψ⁡(xi)=Ψ⁡(yj)\psi(x_{i})=\Psi(y_{j}).

Given ∂∈LND⁡(B)\partial\in\mathrm{LND}(B) and Ψ∈Isom(A,B)k\Psi\in\mathrm{Isom}{}_{k}(A,B). For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have (Ψ−1​∂Ψ)n=Ψ−1​∂nΨ(\Psi^{-1}\partial\Psi)^{n}=\Psi^{-1}\partial^{n}\Psi. So we see that Ψ−1​∂Ψ∈LND⁡(A)\Psi^{-1}\partial\Psi\in\mathrm{LND}(A). An immediate result is Ψ⁡(ML⁡(A))=ML⁡(B)\Psi(\mathrm{ML}(A))=\mathrm{ML}(B) for any Ψ∈Isom(A,B)k\Psi\in\mathrm{Isom}{}_{k}(A,B). Denote ∂Ψ:=Ψ−1∂Ψ\partial_{\Psi}:=\Psi^{-1}\partial\Psi, we have the following properties

  1. (1)

    Ψ{ker(∂Ψ)}=ker(∂)\Psi\{\ker(\partial_{\Psi})\}=\ker(\partial).

  2. (2)

    deg∂Ψ⁡(a)=deg∂⁡(Ψ⁡(a))\deg_{\partial_{\Psi}}(a)=\deg_{\partial}(\Psi(a)) for all a∈Aa\in A.

In [11], Poloni obtained similar results to the next Proposition.

Proposition 6.6.

Let B1=k⁡[x1,y1,z1]B_{1}=k[x_{1},y_{1},z_{1}] and B2=k⁡[x2,y2,z2]B_{2}=k[x_{2},y_{2},z_{2}] be as in 4.1.1 where

P1=y1m1+fm1−2​(x1)​y1m1−2+⋯+f0​(x1)P_{1}=y_{1}^{m_{1}}+f_{m_{1}-2}(x_{1})y_{1}^{m_{1}-2}+\cdots+f_{0}(x_{1})
P2=y2m2+gm2−2​(x2)​y2m2−2+⋯+g0​(x2)P_{2}=y_{2}^{m_{2}}+g_{m_{2}-2}(x_{2})y_{2}^{m_{2}-2}+\cdots+g_{0}(x_{2})

fi​(x1)∈k⁡[x1]f_{i}(x_{1})\in k[x_{1}], gi​(x2)∈k⁡[x2]g_{i}(x_{2})\in k[x_{2}] and ni>1,mi>1n_{i}>1,m_{i}>1. Then

B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} are isomorphic if and only if n=n1=n2n=n_{1}=n_{2}, m=m1=m2m=m_{1}=m_{2}, and fm−i​(λ​x)≡μi​gm−i​(x)f_{m-i}(\lambda x)\equiv\mu^{i}g_{m-i}(x) mod xnx^{n} for every i∈{2,…,m}i\in\{2,\ldots,m\} .

In addition, every isomorphism between B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} takes the form

Ψ⁡(x1,y1,z1)=(λ​x2,μ​y2+x2n​a​(x2),μmλn​z2+P1​(λ​x2,μ​y2+x2n​a​(x2))−μm​P2​(x2,y2)λn​x2n),\Psi(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})=(\lambda x_{2},\,\mu y_{2}+x_{2}^{n}a(x_{2}),\,\frac{\mu^{m}}{\lambda^{n}}z_{2}+\frac{P_{1}(\lambda x_{2},\mu y_{2}+x_{2}^{n}a(x_{2}))-\mu^{m}P_{2}(x_{2},y_{2})}{\lambda^{n}x_{2}^{n}}),

where a⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]a(x)\in k[x] and λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}, μ∈k∗\mu\in k^{*} satisfy fm−i​(λ​x)≡μi​gm−i​(x)f_{m-i}(\lambda x)\equiv\mu^{i}g_{m-i}(x) mod xnx^{n} for all ii.

Proof.

Let D∈LND⁡(B2)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B_{2}), and let Ψ∈Isom(B1,B2)k\Psi\in\mathrm{Isom}{}_{k}(B_{1},B_{2}). By property 2, degDΨ⁡(x1)=degD⁡(Ψ⁡(x1))\deg_{D_{\Psi}}(x_{1})=\deg_{D}(\Psi(x_{1})), but we saw before that degE⁡(x1)=0\deg_{E}(x_{1})=0 for all E∈LND⁡(B1)E\in\mathrm{LND}(B_{1}), so we get degDΨ⁡(x1)=0=degD⁡(Ψ⁡(x1))\deg_{D_{\Psi}}(x_{1})=0=\deg_{D}(\Psi(x_{1})) and Ψ⁡(x1)∈ℱ0=k⁡[x2]\Psi(x_{1})\in\mathcal{F}_{0}=k[x_{2}]. The same argument shows that degDΨ⁡(y1)=1=degD⁡(Ψ⁡(y1))\deg_{D_{\Psi}}(y_{1})=1=\deg_{D}(\Psi(y_{1})), Ψ⁡(y1)∈ℱ1−ℱ0\Psi(y_{1})\in\mathcal{F}_{1}-\mathcal{F}_{0}, and degDΨ⁡(z1)=m1=degD⁡(Ψ⁡(z1))\deg_{D_{\Psi}}(z_{1})=m_{1}=\deg_{D}(\Psi(z_{1})).
